title: Atlas (mythology)
wiki_lead:
In Greek mythology, Atlas (; Ancient Greek: Ἄτλας, romanized: Átlas) is a Titan condemned to hold up the heavens or sky for eternity after the Titanomachy. Atlas also plays a role in the myths of two of the greatest Greek heroes: Heracles (Hercules in Roman mythology) and Perseus. According to the ancient Greek poet Hesiod, Atlas stood at the ends of the earth in the extreme west. Later, he became commonly identified with the Atlas Mountains in northwest Africa. Atlas was said to have been skilled in philosophy, mathematics, and astronomy. In antiquity, he was credited with inventing the first celestial sphere. In some texts, he is even credited with the invention of astronomy itself.
Atlas was the son of the Titan Iapetus and the Oceanid Asia or Clymene. He was a brother of Menoetius, Epimetheus and Prometheus. He had many children, mostly daughters, the Hesperides, the Hyades, the Pleiades, and the nymph Calypso who lived on the island Ogygia.
Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator characterized Atlas as the founder of geography, leading to the modern sense of the term "atlas" for a collection of maps after Mercator published his own work in honor of the Titan.
The "Atlantic Ocean" is derived from "Sea of Atlas." The name of Atlantis mentioned in Plato's Timaeus dialogue derives from "Atlantis nesos" (Ancient Greek: Ἀτλαντὶς νῆσος), literally meaning "Atlantean Island".

Etymology

The etymology of the name Atlas is uncertain. Virgil translated etymologies of Greek names by combining them with adjectives that explained them: for Atlas his adjective is durus, "hard, enduring", which suggested to George Doig that Virgil was aware of the Greek τλῆναι "to endure"; Doig offers the further possibility that Virgil was aware of Strabo's remark that the native North African name for this mountain was Douris. Since the Atlas Mountains rise in the region inhabited by Berbers, it has been suggested that the name might be taken from one of the Berber languages, specifically from the word ádrār "mountain".
Traditionally historical linguists etymologize the Ancient Greek word Ἄτλας (genitive: Ἄτλαντος) as comprised from copulative α- and the Proto-Indo-European root *telh₂- 'to uphold, support' (whence also τλῆναι), and which was later reshaped to an nt-stem. However, Robert S. P. Beekes argues that it cannot be expected that this ancient Titan carries an Indo-European name, and he suggests instead that the word is of Pre-Greek origin, as such words often end in -ant.


Mythology


War and punishment

Atlas and his brother Menoetius sided with the Titans in their war against the Olympians, the Titanomachy. When the Titans were defeated, many of them (including Menoetius) were confined to Tartarus, but Zeus condemned Atlas to stand at the western edge of the earth and hold up the sky on his shoulders. Thus, he was Atlas Telamon, "enduring Atlas", and became a doublet of Coeus, the embodiment of the celestial axis around which the heavens revolve.

grok_lead: In Greek mythology, Atlas is a Titan and leader of his kind, condemned by Zeus to bear the weight of the heavens upon his shoulders for eternity following his defeat in the Titanomachy, the war between the Titans and the Olympian gods. As the son of the Titan Iapetus and the Oceanid Clymene, Atlas embodies endurance and is often depicted at the western edge of the world, near the Hesperides, upholding the sky with unweary hands to prevent its collapse onto the earth. He is also characterized as a figure of profound knowledge, particularly of the sea's depths and the pillars that separate heaven and earth, earning him the epithet of a "baleful-minded" being in early accounts. Atlas's role extends beyond his punishment, as he fathered several notable offspring, including the Pleiades (seven nymph daughters transformed into stars), the Hyades (nymphs associated with rain), the Hesperides (guardians of a golden apple orchard), and the nymph Calypso, who detained Odysseus on her island. In prominent myths, Atlas interacts with heroes: during Heracles 's eleventh labor to retrieve the golden apple s of the Hesperides, he temporarily relieved Heracles of the celestial burden to fetch the fruit himself, only to be tricked into resuming it when Heracles used the apples as leverage. Later traditions describe Perseus turning Atlas to stone with Medusa's head, transforming him into the Atlas Mountains of North Africa. These narratives highlight Atlas's enduring legacy as a symbol of strength, suffering, and the boundaries of the cosmos in classical literature.
